title: With Melania , We See Nothing
excerpt: “Do you ever think about death?” Brett Ratner asks Melania Trump, midway through the second and final episode of Melania: The Series (as opposed to Melania , th
body: “Do you ever think about death?” Brett Ratner asks Melania Trump, midway through the second and final episode of Melania: The Series (as opposed to Melania , the movie , or Melania , the memoir , or $Melania , the cryptocurrency )

Melania—typing her name this many times in a row has given me a dizzying feeling of semantic satiation—is sitting on Air Force One, shot in tight focus, wearing a black jacket and a faint scowl. “Of course you think about it,” she replies, revealing teeth so white, they’re almost blue. “You just want to make sure that, you know, the family or my child are taken care of
It’s very in, um, it’s in the stars.” And with that, the question is dismissed, the specter of mortality diffused as rapidly as air from a popped balloon

I can’t say I felt for Ratner, exactly, watching all one hour and 11 minutes of Melania: The Series , because if it weren’t for the allegations of sexual harassment and assault made against him in 2017 (allegations that he denies), he wouldn’t have been exiled to creative Siberia and I wouldn’t have spent multiple hours watching Melania (the Trump) gliding purposefully into the spa at Mar-a-Lago or describing the many exciting benefits that blockchain provides for her fan base

But I’ve spent enough time interviewing resistant subjects to recognize the desperation kicking in as he realizes he’s got nothing . “Have you ever slept in?” he asks at one point. (Not really.) “Do you ever take long walks?” (She doesn’t.) “Do you have a favorite book?” (It’s Melania , of course.) All the while, the camera stays trained on his subject, her eyebrows penciled heavily in two straight lines as if to minimize any human expression she might otherwise convey

Much has been made of how stultifying Melania: The Series is as a televisual experience—how devoid of action! How recycled of content! How toadying in approach! But the series’ emptiness also feels illuminating, in a metatextual kind of way
Ratner gives us such relentless footage of Melania, posed and composed and airtight, that he brings the whole project of documentary filmmaking into disarray

What does it mean to watch someone for such prolonged periods of time and see nothing at all? Every day, we are awash in images and clips—“We sleep and eat the image and pray to it and wear it too,” as Don DeLillo wrote in Mao II . (As if to offer proof, in one scene in Melania: The Series , an assistant director clambers out from behind the camera to show Melania a photo of everything his brother rescued from his house in Los Angeles before it burned down in the 2025 wildfires—his guitars and his MAGA hats.) The president is a booster of artificially generated imagery, which tends to suit his particular aesthetic: gaudy, emotionally staged, ideological

And the most dominant movie of the moment is a documentary, You Can See Everything , which, like Melania , manipulates the visual and aural language of film, but as anti-propaganda, to show us how profoundly untrustworthy it has been all along
In that nearly three-hour movie, by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, Elizabeth Holmes’s face, like Melania’s, absorbs the camera
Fielder moves in with the disgraced Theranos founder and her partner, Billy Evans, in the weeks before she goes to prison for fraud
Holmes seems to be under the impression that through what Evans calls “radical transparency” she can persuade Fielder, and the rest of us, of her innocence

And so, for a few weeks, a pair of the most practiced illusionists in American culture go head-to-head in her rented, wood-paneled beach house: the Silicon Valley saleswoman and the comedian so committed to the bit that he once trained for almost two and a half years to become a commercial pilot, in service of his TV show
Two manipulators, each alike in proficiency
The question seems to be less about which one will prevail—Fielder has the lopsided power of final cut—than about whether anything unexpected will be revealed in the process

From the beginning, Fielder and Oppenheim use angles and lighting to set up stock roles: Holmes, the mother clutching an infant, awash in natural light, is the heroine; Fielder, lurking in the darkness and grimacing, is her antagonist
Her face is almost ludicrously likable on camera, rubberized and wide-eyed, guileless, and the movie zooms in on it well past the point of discomfort
Holmes weeps, she breaks down, she locks eyes with Fielder so intently that the pair seem to be glued to each other

All this looking gives Fielder no insight into what to make of her, so in the second half of the film, after she goes to jail, he restages scenes of their meetings and even seeks the help of a professional actor to try to get inside her head

Holmes remains unknowable, much as Melania does, despite all the time we’ve spent watching her , despite the “equivocal magic” of the image, as Susan Sontag once wrote, and despite the fact that You Can See Everything uses scenes and images to provoke every emotional response in the handbook: shock (unexpected full-frontal nudity), pathos (a devastated Holmes being led into prison), suspense (Hitchcockian angles and shadows)
The score, by Ari Balouzian, all jagged strings and low, discordant humming, similarly seems intent on trying to make us feel
For all of its prolonged run time, the movie is riveting
But it also clearly lays its tricks on the table: Storytelling is a fundamentally manipulative process, Fielder seems to argue by the end
Ratner uses many of the same techniques as Fielder to elicit emotion in Melania —heavy-handed aural hooks, close-ups, shameless scenes of devastation
He comes up short, but perhaps that’s because he lacks the true skill of canny scammers and filmmakers: sensing what people, in all our glorious and idiotic humanity, really want to see.

title: Here Comes Santa Claude
excerpt: When Cynthia Bell McGillis needs help with her holiday shopping, she turns to Mrs
body: When Cynthia Bell McGillis needs help with her holiday shopping, she turns to Mrs
Not the one in the North Pole, but her own custom-built AI agent

After getting a head start on buying Christmas presents last month, McGillis had an idea of how to more easily keep track of her purchases: “I bet Grok can help with that,” McGillis, who works in marketing for an AI start-up in San Diego, told me
She instructed Grok Bot, an AI assistant made by Elon Musk, to constantly scan her email inbox every day. “Mrs
Claus” now logs arriving items and who they are for, searches the newsletters McGillis subscribes to for sales on potential gift ideas, and keeps a running total of how much McGillis has spent
The day we spoke, the bot had just surfaced a discount on Old Navy Christmas-themed pajamas
In recent months, tech companies have launched a number of AI personal assistants, one after the other
Instinct, an agent that allows users to chat with it directly from the iMessage app, went viral in August ; the next month, Meta launched its competitor, Muse
According to Mark Zuckerberg, more than 10 million users tried Muse in its first six weeks

Unlike traditional chatbots, AI agents can act on your behalf in the real world: Feed them your credit-card information and online passwords (if you dare), and they can find restaurant reservations, book flights, and, yes, buy gifts on your behalf
This month, OpenAI debuted ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its agents to also make purchases for users. [ Read: AI agents are here
Nobody’s ready. ] Now, for the first time, some people are about to open presents that were chosen and purchased entirely by bots
When Rohit Bakshi, an AI-product director in the Bay Area, wanted to get his nephew a Tin Can, the popular Wi-Fi-enabled “landline” for kids , he messaged Instinct to buy it

Bakshi told me that using Instinct more for holiday shopping would be a “no-brainer.” I heard similar enthusiasm from Boaz Sobrado, a tech worker also based in the Bay Area. (Every agentic-AI-loving shopper I could find had some connection to the tech industry.) Sobrado recently asked his girlfriend’s Muse agent, which knows her Instagram likes and saved posts, to find a hotel that matched her tastes

Agents can crawl through hundreds of text messages and emails to identify a tailored gift—something the intended recipient mentioned a long time ago, maybe, or something they might like based on contextual clues
AI companies are certainly invested in the notion that their personal assistants can be heroes this holiday season

In an email, Ben Schwerin, the chief business officer of Instinct, told me that the company has seen a recent uptick in people using its agents to shop. “What’s been interesting is people are trusting Instinct to complete purchases for a full gift list, rather than handing Instinct one-off links,” he said

Meanwhile, Meta is partnering with social-media influencers to tout how Muse can be used for holiday shopping, such as by choosing gifts on a budget. (Meta declined to answer questions about how people are using Muse for holiday shopping.) Americans without ties to the tech industry so far seem less bought in
AI assistants, for the most part, have yet to fully enter the mainstream

Some of that gap may be principled: Much of the country, after all, remains concerned about AI’s rapid development, and people certainly have good reason to be uncomfortable with the idea of a bot shopping with their credit card and having detailed access to their family’s personal information
AI assistants can also be expensive, many requiring subscriptions that run more than $100 a month
Some major retailers, including Amazon, have banned AI agents; the e-commerce giant is reportedly worried about what shopping bots could mean for its advertising business
The promise of convenience can be hard to ignore
Lots of people who aren’t using agents to shop on their behalf are still asking AI for gift-giving help
This year, 40 percent of shoppers say they plan to use generative AI for holiday shopping, such as by asking ChatGPT for product recommendations, according to a recent report from Accenture
Kath Gramling, who leads the consumer-goods-and-retail division at Accenture, believes that many people who use LLMs may soon adopt AI agents too. “It’s just a natural extension,” Gramling told me
More shoppers may soon experience what can go wrong when you let an AI personal assistant run wild

One man claimed on X that his AI agent accidentally posted his bank-account balances in a Slack channel at his workplace; another man told Business Insider that a request for ingredients to make dinner for two resulted in a 20-pound chicken-wing order
Indeed, not all of Sobrado’s purchases have been successful: He recently ordered flowers for his girlfriend using his Muse agent, which he named Hermenegildo

When the flowers arrived, he realized that the agent had attached a card for his girlfriend and signed it, With love, Hermenegildo . [ Read: It’s all fun and games until you give AI your credit card ] Even if you aren’t using an AI personal assistant to buy any gifts, the bots might still affect your holiday-shopping experience

Last month, a Verge reporter wrote that she was able to instruct her Muse agent to continuously hold items in her cart on the RealReal, blocking other potential shoppers from purchasing them on the secondhand-luxury-fashion website. (Following the report, the RealReal said that the company would make it more difficult for agents to shop on its website.) And yesterday, Walmart announced that the company will now let Muse agents browse for deals and make purchases on users’ behalf
Black Fridays of decades past were an endurance game of who could wake up at the crack of dawn and brave the freezing weather in pursuit of a deal
This Black Friday might be a competition of who has the best AI agent
All of this raises the age-old holiday question: What is gift giving really for ? AI agents will never be able to replicate the experiential aspects of holiday magic
I love spending weeks clicking through websites until I feel the eureka moment of finding the perfect gift that I know someone will love
Others enjoy walking in a physical mall during the holidays, past the twinkling lights and smiling Santa

Bakshi told me that he can’t imagine letting Instinct do all of his holiday shopping. “I like going to the stores,” he said. “There’s a lot of festivity to it.” The principle stands that a Christmas gift is supposed to symbolize the love and appreciation you feel for a recipient
Instead, gift-giving frequently becomes a matter of commercialism and obligation
Now AI agents are opening the possibility of delivering incredibly personal gifts with about the same effort it takes to purchase a gift card
Hopefully for gift givers, they’ll get everyone’s name right.

title: How Did Any Child Survive the 1970s?
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum is joined by the author and journa
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum is joined by the author and journalist Meghan Cox Gurdon to discuss her new memoir, Free Range Girl , about growing up in the 1970s
They explore how parenting has changed, the risks and rewards of childhood freedom, and why the past may not deserve our rose-colored nostalgia
The following is a transcript of the episode: Meghan Cox Gurdon: I would say that parents today would be arrested for half the things—for almost anything that we were allowed to do
The social norms were so different back in the day. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic
And for this Thanksgiving edition of The David Frum Show , I’ll be talking to Meghan Cox Gurdon, author of a new memoir of growing up in the 1970s, Free Range Girl
At the end of the show, I’ll offer some personal words of thanks to you, the viewers and listeners of The David Frum Show
But before either the conclusion thanks or the dialogue, I want to talk at the beginning about why I invited Meghan Cox Gurdon to come and discuss her memoir of life in the 1970s
I was inspired by a 2026 poll conducted by NBC News that found that nearly half of adults ages 18 to 29 said that, if they had the option, they would choose to live in the past
They meant the recent past: the 1970s or the 1990s, about which they have all kinds of nostalgic feelings
So I wanted to tell them: I was there, and while definitely, like, the dating apps are making things worse and social media is a nuisance and AI is a little menacing, you do not wish you were there
I remember during the birther controversy of the Obama years when people had this fantasy that President Obama was born in Kenya
Remember that? Now, we know that President Obama’s mother was present in Hawaii, attending school, in the spring of the year that he was born, 1961
The theory of the case was that she somehow got from Hawaii to Kenya to give birth to the president and came back
But I took my first airplane flight in the middle 1960s with my parents, and I can remember some of those flights
I just want to conjure up what it would have been like for the young mother of President Obama to do this
I imagine a travel agent saying to her: Very well, Ms
Honolulu to Los Angeles; Los Angeles to New York; New York to London; London to Nairobi
The Honolulu–Los Angeles leg of the trip by itself —and I looked this up— will cost more than a semester’s tuition at the University of Hawaii
You’ll have to pay by cash or certified check, since it’s exceedingly unlikely you qualify for American Express or Diners Club, as no other credit card yet exists
Bring plenty to read, since the in-flight movie has also only just been invented
I see you’re nine months pregnant, so you might ask the stewardess to seat you beside a passenger who doesn’t smoke
I hope your life insurance is up to date, since the risk of passenger fatality per mile is nearly 1,000 times greater than it will be in 2026
I mean, what were they thinking? How would that be? But they don’t remember
They don’t remember the world before seat belts
They don’t remember the world of universal smoking
I don’t even understand quite how any of us who were children in the 1960s and ’70s got out alive

One of the defining experiences of our childhoods was riding in a front seat beside an adult, and when a car in front of you braked, the adult would fling out an arm. ( Laughs. ) As if somehow their arm would stop you from crashing into the hard metal headboard that would otherwise bash you in

But you really don’t want to live there, and Meghan Gurdon and I will discuss why not in the segment that we’re about to begin. [ Music ] Frum: In 1976, the year America turned 200, a 12-year-old girl left her mother’s home in New York and moved to rural Maine to live with her father
He was a back-to-the-land man, and he had built the house himself
The little girl bathed in a tin tub and carried spring water in by the bucket to heat on the stove
That year, the girl rode horses bareback, and one of them threw her
She was found face down in a field with a concussion and two black eyes
She burned her eyebrows off lighting an oven while babysitting her little cousin
She grew up to become a foreign correspondent, and since 2005 she has been the children’s book critic of The Wall Street Journal
She is the author of The Enchanted Hour , about why reading aloud matters
Her new book is the story of that year in Maine in 1976
The book is about freedom, and also about what freedom costs; a childhood without screens or supervision among adults who are often busy with their own lives
We hear a lot of arguments about how today’s children are raised
Meghan has lived on both sides of that argument—first as the child in the story, and then as the parent of five children herself

title: I’m Not Going to Play Grand Theft Auto VI
excerpt: As a member of the puritan third of Americans who do not play video games, I’ve been disoriented by the hoopla around the release of Grand Theft Auto VI , but a
body: As a member of the puritan third of Americans who do not play video games, I’ve been disoriented by the hoopla around the release of Grand Theft Auto VI , but also mesmerized by it
This is, I imagine, how it feels to be in a foreign country as it celebrates a national holiday you only dimly understand
People smile and make loud noises and engage in cheerful rituals that are as mysterious as they are, evidently, important

From reading the extensive coverage of GTA 6 —and hearing about the broader franchise over the years from acquaintances who play it—I do know this: Grand Theft Auto is a series of games in which players wander around replicas of various cities committing crimes, including robbing banks, stealing cars, selling drugs, and killing civilians and police officers

And this latest installment is, according to a swiftly building early consensus, very, very good. [ Read: ] Grand Theft Auto VI is really weird Reviews of the game in both mainstream and gaming outlets have declared it a “masterpiece” that is at once a penetrating satire of American excess and a tender romance
Critics have noted in particular how much more mature GTA 6 is than previous iterations of the franchise, which debuted in 1997
Gone, for example, are the beddable (and killable) prostitutes—a controversial mainstay of the earlier games
Instead, players work to maintain a relationship between the protagonist, Jason, and his girlfriend, Lucia
As Jason, a player can hold hands with Lucia, paint and clean their house in preparation for her release from jail, and engage in pleasant mundanities such as grocery shopping

You can even lie in bed next to Lucia and doomscroll on your phone. “Much of what you can do—apart from activities routine to G.T.A. like stealing cars and robbing banks—is taking action to care for and nurture your romantic partner,” a New York Times reviewer wrote
I don’t doubt that the game is, as its boosters claim, arresting and disarming in its opportunities for compassion
Perhaps it is even “ high art ,” as one review declared

But for all the praise GTA 6 is receiving, I’m not tempted to buy a console and join the gaming masses, and I can’t help but feel uneasy that legions of adults are spending their time and money on this spectacle
For one thing, the game is still incredibly violent, despite its new focus on domesticity: The thieving, drug dealing, and innocent-bystander-murdering remain

One clip of the game, which shows a player conducting a mass shooting at a hospital, has been viewed more than 25 million times on X, in a thread that includes other in-game mass shootings at an airport, at a police station, and on a downtown street

Defenders of the franchise have claimed that this hyper-violence is the backbone of what is actually “a sharp, progressive satire” that exposes society’s wickedness by turning the dial on that wickedness up to 11

It’s a familiar argument, one that has been used frequently to justify artworks that explore humanity’s basest tendencies. [ Read: The right way to adapt a video game ] Many art genres—including some I like a great deal—use depictions of extreme violence as a form of social critique: gangster rap, death metal, horror movies, and so on
But a crucial difference between these works and a video game such as GTA 6 is that they do not require their audiences to reenact depravity
Gamers like to point out that violent video games do not seem to inspire players to enact real-world harm, and this is true
They also point out that many people who play games are productive members of society—good parents, partners, friends, and employees

But surely “Does this product lead to real-world homicidal rage?” or “Does this activity sabotage most people’s personal lives?” are rather low bars to clear, and not the only metrics for evaluating whether something is worthwhile, let alone moral

Wells, or Aldous Huxley, or any of the great early-20th-century dystopian sci-fi writers that, in the 21st century, large segments of the adult population would spend much of their free time glued to a crime-and-murder simulator, they would have recognized what you are describing as a kind of dystopia
What’s more, violence aside, GTA 6 is like every other video game in that it requires players to sit on their couch and give their undivided attention to the screen

I cannot kick the gut-level suspicion that has led me to keep my distance from video games throughout my adult life: Here is an island for lotus eating, one that invites you to waste away on its virtual soil
The fact that this particular game has high-minded aspirations, and maybe lives up to them, doesn’t mean that the lotus isn’t there waiting for you

Many modern video games, after all, have extensive, sophisticated design features that are purpose-built to keep players playing, and to disincentivize logging off, in a way that other immersive hobbies—including, say, reading novels, or bingeing television shows, or spending all of Sunday watching NFL games—do not

With GTA 6 , the medium remains the message, and the legitimate praise of this new game’s content seems to obscure the reality of its form: the controller, the couch, the screen, the hours in their grip. “I never want to leave,” PCMag ’s Jordan Minor wrote
And isn’t that the very point and the very problem? GTA 6 cannot help but drain the distance between its critique of American life and much of what it criticizes
It satirizes the glorification of violence even as it offers violence as entertainment
It asks players to contemplate what it means to try to get your life together, even as droves of adults, here in the real world, take paid time off to play PlayStation

It asks men to consider what it means to be a good boyfriend, even as many of the men playing it are almost certainly neglecting their very real girlfriends and families and wives to do so. “Your bf is booking the day off work to do chores for his little game wife,” one woman joked on X

title: What Could Replace the Trump Style of Politics?
excerpt: J onathan Spector’s play Birthright , which had a recent off-Broadway run, crescendos with what can best be described as a Google duel
body: J onathan Spector’s play Birthright , which had a recent off-Broadway run, crescendos with what can best be described as a Google duel
In the last act, which takes place in 2024, the nearly two-decade bond between a group of American Jewish friends has frayed over Gaza
Izzy, the most left-wing of the bunch, has already abandoned their online group chat, where the friends shared photos of their newborn children, checked in during COVID, and planned their reunions
Thrown together for a funeral, Izzy and another friend, Chaya, begin to argue—as one does these days—about Zionism

They quickly whip out their phones, mustering evidence. “Theodor Herzl colonialism,” Izzy types into the search window, which—in an ingenious bit of stagecraft—appears projected on the wall behind her and starts to flow with online sources. “1930s partition plan Israel,” Chaya counter-Googles
They start scrolling through newspaper articles and Wikipedia pages, hurling raw historical information at each other like malfunctioning robots

Their friend Noah, watching from the side, offers that going to the internet to prove your point is useless because you’ll invariably find what you’re looking for—“which is why I think this is really, really not a good way to go about having an actual conversation.” This mode of political discourse is surely familiar: the search for a truth that will detonate like an atom bomb, ripping the roof off every other truth
Most of us know that this outcome never, ever happens
But beneath the awareness of information bubbles and fake news, of epistemic breakdown, lies a stubbornly common belief that total victory is achievable

This fantasy has even become its own kind of entertainment—think of Jubilee Media ’s viral videos in which one person has to fend off 20 political opponents like a medieval knight, or the late Charlie Kirk ’s “Prove Me Wrong” college tours

Theories are packed tight with facts and lobbed back and forth in what the German philosopher Hannah Arendt once called “an orgy of truth-telling.” Arendt used this strange phrase in a 1946 letter to the philosopher Gershom Scholem, her dear intellectual sparring partner, after they had gotten into a fierce argument about—what else?—Zionism
One shouldn’t be a “fanatic for truth,” Arendt told him
All this did was harden people in their positions: I have my truth, you have yours, and the only way forward is for you to admit that not just your opinions but your facts are wrong
This is no way to hold a debate, or to conduct politics; all it does is create stasis or even worse

Elsewhere, Arendt called truth in this context “despotic.” She argued instead for a different mode, one that would be surprising—okay, maybe fantastical—to consider today: “an orgy of friendship.” In a recently published book, A World We Share , Roger Berkowitz explores the German philosopher’s thoughts on friendship “as the lens through which she understood politics.” For Arendt, who is best known for her hard-bitten analysis of totalitarianism, friendship might seem to be an uncharacteristically schmaltzy subject, but as filtered through her mind, abstracted and held apart, it sheds all Hallmark associations

Berkowitz, the director of the Hannah Arendt Center for Politics and Humanities at Bard College, provides the material for an intriguing thought experiment, one that might be useful as Americans rub their eyes in the post-midterms dawn

After a decade in which Donald Trump’s tribalist instincts have only accelerated that rush to Google-dueling, it might be worth pursuing Arendt’s idea that friendship, as opposed to truth-telling, is a better model for conducting politics
A rendt never left behind a treatise on friendship, but references to the concept pop up throughout her work and letters
Berkowitz, who has a granular familiarity with her writing, brings all of the strands together
For Arendt, friendship is distinct from love as we often think of it; it is not about losing yourself in order to meld with another person and separate from the rest of the world
Instead, this kind of connection preserves difference and feeds off plurality

Friendship is actually the most worldly of relationships because it forces us to accommodate the separateness of the people we know and care about. [ Read: It’s the morality, stupid ] Arendt articulated three defining features: time spent knowing each other (“a two-week-old friendship does not exist,” she said); talking and more talking and even more talking; and a respect and appreciation for the unique conditions that shape someone else’s worldview

This kind of friendship, she thought, should withstand even the most violent disagreements. “A human being is far more valuable than his opinions,” she wrote in her letter to Scholem, begging that they not lose their connection despite her public disillusionment with the idea of an exclusively Jewish state—a critique Scholem must have felt as a body blow

Berkowitz points out that for Arendt, what makes us human “is not our ability to reason or our grasp of moral certainty or absolute truth but our ability to form lasting and meaningful relationships grounded in mutual recognition and respect.” The fact that she and Scholem had spent more than a decade talking, listening, and yelling was more important to her than any need for them to come to similar conclusions
Her emphasis was rather on this “in-between,” the “common world” they shared and built just by continuing to engage on the issues that mattered to them both
Could any of this possibly be applicable to America’s political culture, which most days resembles the fear and loathing of trench warfare? Dream with me for a minute

Imagine if arguments at Thanksgiving dinner or in Congress proceeded with an awareness that conquering the other person’s worldview was impossible—in the way you can’t really change that old friend who keeps dating the wrong people
Imagine if the goal was to tease out commonalities, instead of trying to will the differences away
This type of politics would be fueled by persuasion, as opposed to force or truth, Berkowitz writes; it would aim “neither at domination nor certainty
It is not about being right.” Arendt’s favored metaphor for this in-between is a table around which people with disparate views and interests sit
The existence of the table matters more than anyone’s particular opinions
The American version of this table does exist, however alienated we may feel from one another
The changing state of the economy, for example, or the future of children’s education, are issues that could potentially be served at this table
Some topics—say, abortion rights—would produce more heat, maybe some fist-pounding
But if the objective is to make sure that the table itself doesn’t evaporate, the conversation might continue
Certain shared worries from our shared world will present themselves as commonalities, even as people’s perspectives remain distinct

Take the proliferation of data centers or the cost of health care. “By talking about what is between them,” Arendt writes, friends and citizens can make that shared world “ever more common.” [ Read: Why we should read Hannah Arendt now ] This is what an orgy of friendship (as opposed to one of truth) could look like
I don’t have any illusions that this shift of mindset is easy

But some politicians could point the way—for instance Senator-Elect James Talarico of Texas. “I really do believe that the key to saving the American experiment is loving our enemies,” he recently told Michelle Goldberg at The New York Times . “How do we love each other through our disagreements? How do we remember each other’s humanity? How do we handle each other with more care?” Talarico gives this a Christian gloss with his talk of “love,” which is not quite what Arendt had in mind, but she would otherwise be sympathetic to his willingness to make friends with those who have been calling him “Talafreako” for the past year
Of course, going to Washington could very well crush this friendliness out of him, but it is worth paying attention to how rhetorically effective his approach has been

title: The Surprising Pleasures of Aging Gracefully
excerpt: “I hope I die before I get old,” a 21-year-old Roger Daltrey famously sneered on the Who’s 1965 single “My Generation.” At the time, the countercultural upshot
body: “I hope I die before I get old,” a 21-year-old Roger Daltrey famously sneered on the Who’s 1965 single “My Generation.” At the time, the countercultural upshot was clear: Music was a young man’s game, especially rock and roll
Rock music embodied rebellion and fearlessness
It was about spitting in the face of elders who disapproved of what they could never understand

Who could trust a rock star still playing those kinds of songs well into middle age? Of course, the surviving members of the Who are now in their 80s and still performing, despite promises of retirement, because the benefits of playing decades-old songs to adoring crowds remain strong
The expectation of releasing new music has faded away
Audiences come to bask in memories from their youth or share their passions with their kids
Classic rockers such as the Who, the Rolling Stones, and the Eagles set the template for hugely profitable late-in-life reunion tours; successive generations of bands have followed suit
Now the cycle continues with two defining British bands from the mid-’90s, who have reunited to remind the public that the music from the Britpop era was really just that good

Two new documentaries about Oasis and Pulp, inspired by their respective circa-2025 tours, capture the spirit of the bands while digging into how they’ve processed the passage of time—to fascinating effect

Oasis was the most successful of the Britpop groups; led by the brothers Noel and Liam Gallagher, its swaggering rock music conveyed the maximalist melodrama of being young and in love with women, drugs, and ambition
Pulp was arguably the coolest Britpop group, whose front man, Jarvis Cocker, led with a sly, eccentric style and literary sensibility that stood in sharp contrast to his noisier peers

Like the Gallaghers, he seemed to genuinely relish his celebrity, but his relatively reserved personality made his indulgences seem chic and deliberate—potential grist for the lyrical mill, not simply rock-and-roll decadence
Don’t Look Back in Anger chronicles the highly anticipated Oasis reunion tour in 2025 that rejuvenated the band’s public image, following an acrimonious 2009 split
What Do You Do for an Encore? , for its part, combines a traditional concert film with a snapshot survey of Pulp’s lengthy career, and is narrated with wry humor by Cocker himself

Both documentaries attempt to bridge the gap between nostalgia for a past heyday and sanguine acceptance of a hazy future, while asking a simple yet difficult question: How do rock and rollers grow old without embarrassing themselves? In the ’90s, the British music media spent a lot of time publicizing an astroturfed competition between Oasis and its fellow chart-topper Blur , its baroque, Anglophilic-pop counterpart
Amid this sniping, Pulp stood apart as the round peg in a sea of square holes

A working-class kid from Sheffield, Cocker was 31 when Pulp’s best-known single, “Common People,” climbed the U.K. charts in 1995, making him something of an elder statesman relative to his musical peers
Draped in dapper outfits accentuating his lanky frame, Cocker represented an androgynous, cerebral alternative to the era’s boisterous masculinity
What Do You Do for an Encore? sketches out how Cocker graduated from a teenage outsider to a patron saint for sensitive, horny misfits

The documentary is anchored by performances from Pulp’s sold-out shows at London’s O2 Arena in June 2025 and is interspersed with “commercial breaks” during which Cocker, in voice-over, cheekily breaks the fourth wall to narrate his early childhood and experiences with fame
The film highlights Cocker’s alt-lothario stage presence as he sings about a world of hedonism and heartbreak, coming off as a veteran actor who’s only grown deeper into his role

In contrast, Don’t Look Back in Anger ’s directors, Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern, frequently cut away from Oasis’s performances to focus on the crowd itself, singling out individuals in tears or mid-embrace
They also incorporate numerous testimonials about how Oasis affected fans’ lives
Some are compact voice-over explanations about the power of friendship or self-confidence

Others are longer on-screen tributes, including one from a South Korean haenyeo (a female diver responsible for harvesting sea life) who explains how Oasis’s music gave her the strength to plunge into the water
Another features a survivor of the 2017 Manchester Arena bombing, who discusses how the song that gives the documentary its name helped her process survivor’s guilt
The film also goes to some lengths to imply that the Gallaghers’ reunion mended the culture at large, or at least provided the world with sufficient escapism and hope

Early in the film, Liam says, “When Oasis split up, things just went shit,” which is followed by a montage of news footage that includes the January 6 riots, Donald Trump dancing at a MAGA rally, and a food-delivery robot getting hit by a car. (No montage of positive world events following the tour is to be found.) Later, a Manchester priest speaks to a sparsely attended congregation about how crowds of Oasis fans resemble a pilgrimage and indicate a “shared longing for healing.” The message is clear: No matter what else has happened, the world is better with Oasis in it
Patience for this level of hyperbole obviously depends on the viewer’s affection for Oasis
As a longtime listener, I often found myself chafing against some of the overwrought fan reactions, despite their transparent sincerity
But I can attest to the accuracy of how the film portrays the public fervor that the Oasis reunion inspired in the U.K
In the days leading up to the Dublin show, my friends and I could not walk a few feet in the city without seeing an Oasis T-shirt or bucket hat
The show itself was pandemonium, with approximately 80,000 people singing along to every word of every song

I rarely attend concerts that are on this scale and get this level of hype, so at times I simply watched the crowd move in almost otherworldly unison. “I’d never come across an atmosphere like that at a concert before,” remarked Cocker, who attended one of Oasis’s Wembley shows. “It was like being at some kind of religious rally or something
It was amazing.” Oasis has been the subject of other documentaries, but my favorite is 2016’s Supersonic
The film is laser-focused on the Gallagher brothers’ conversational interplay, which, by default, makes it one of the funniest music documentaries ever released

Hearing Noel and Liam trade barbs about the other’s professional acumen or recount the same drug-fueled period in radically different terms, you might think that their real talent was giving hilarious interviews that exemplified their vulgar charisma
This time around, Noel and Liam—who have recently reconciled amidst years of estrangement—don’t exchange insults

Rather, the film chronicles their growing appreciation for each other as the tour transpires, which is expressed in hand-holding and hugs onstage. “It was all forgiven without saying a word,” Noel says of their beef, a notable reversal
They are older, softer men, who routinely express their gratitude for the opportunity to play 30-year-old songs to sold-out stadiums

title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
excerpt: Data centers are fueling a natural-gas surge: Natural gas has essentially become America's default electricity solution to meet rising demand, including fr
body: Data centers are fueling a natural-gas surge: Natural gas has essentially become America's default electricity solution to meet rising demand, including from data centers
Nearly half the capacity of new proposals in the country's largest grid came from gas plants

Big tech's emissions are climbing fast: Meta's greenhouse-gas emissions jumped 45% in a single year — outpacing Google, Amazon, and Microsoft — and the company is quietly reconsidering its 2030 net-zero commitment

Companies are building their own power plants: Unable to wait for grid connections, data center developers have proposed over 100 off-grid gas facilities since early 2025, with combined capacity more than double California's peak electricity demand. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149836" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas
Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right
Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries
But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence
Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too
The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10
And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants
How did we get here? If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system
In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today
But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC
PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals
In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue
Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue
PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US

Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.  This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies
Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report
That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% )
The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead
It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power
Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well)
Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source
But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers
Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California)
The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025
There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example
I’ve also written before about demand flexibility —efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter
To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

Find out how AI is testing the limits of America’s right to know . —Matthew King MIT Technology Review Narrated: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and soil insulating the permafrost below
Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground
Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases
Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle

title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
excerpt: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all
body: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all
He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer
During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests
Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper
Last year, those requests started coming quarterly
Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares

These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”  Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US
While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest

Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments
At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests
Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years

While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.  As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.  Transparency, monetized The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law
Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools

But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.  This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days

Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “ FOIA, Inc .” Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration
What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says
SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data
Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies
The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer

Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks
The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors

Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”  While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data

For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada
That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites
NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment
The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI
But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices
In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job

Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell
In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says
A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used
FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day , she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year
The AI detection problem It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests

Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection

David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025

The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.  In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests
Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula

But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.  While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests
Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance
Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages

title: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
url:
<title>Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773171/original/file-20261119-62-t0qpui.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=2052%2C0%2C2888%2C1925&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Monks Mound towers over the land at the Cahokia archaeological complex in Illinois.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Monk%27s_mound_panorama.jpg">TimVickers via Wikimedia Commons</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was <a href="https://www.isas.illinois.edu/research_2/cahokia">once home to 20,000 people</a> near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.</p>

<p>My anthropology colleague <a href="https://www.anthropology.wisc.edu/staff/schroeder-sissel/">Sissel Schroeder</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=k4JPb8wAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">I</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaa.2026.101797">studied both sites</a> to learn how people react to climate change when it hits home.  </p>



<h2>Archaeological sites forming in a modern community</h2>

<p>During the 1960s and 1970s, economic downturns and the movement of white residents out of diversifying neighborhoods made Centreville into a majority-Black community that faced challenges such as <a href="https://www.floodedandforgotten.com/history-of-the-centreville-sewage-crisis">mismanaged drainage infrastructure</a>. Yet in <a href="https://www.floodedandforgotten.com/interviews">interviews with a community group, residents reported</a> that people had no major problems with living there until the floods came. </p>

<p><iframe id="geFJ9" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/geFJ9/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Three line charts that show total precipitation, average temperature and population numbers."></iframe></p>

<p>From the 1960s to the 2020s, average annual rainfall in the St. Louis region has increased by <a href="https://www.weather.gov/media/lsx/climate/stl/precip/precip_stl_ranked_annual_amounts.pdf">10 inches</a> (25 centimeters) to 44 inches (112 cm) a year. That has led to more <a href="https://www.bostonreview.net/articles/walter-johnson-detroit-tk/">frequent flooding</a>, including in Centreville, where stormwater and sewage systems have not been significantly updated since they were built in the 1960s. The rains bring floods, which <a href="https://www.floodedandforgotten.com/">back up raw sewage</a> into people’s kitchen sinks, and seep up through the ground, covering residents’ lawns as well as public streets and sidewalks.</p>

<p>Many people who can afford to move away from Centreville have done so, <a href="https://www.stltoday.com/news/local/illinois/a-plea-for-help-centreville-s-sewage-and-drainage-problems-pose-health-safety-risks/article_3d6d22c7-8c57-5d1a-8af3-a6e6ee6ea2ee.html">leaving a mostly older population and many abandoned homes</a>. Essentially, a community is becoming an archaeological site before our eyes.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of photos show buildings in varying degrees of disrepair." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=423&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=423&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=423&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=531&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=531&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773150/original/file-20261119-76-3latv9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=531&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Street-view photos of Centreville show abandoned (A, B) and demolished (C) houses, structure foundations (D,E) and a school building (F,G) that has since been demolished.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaa.2026.101797">White and Schroeder, 2026.</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>An ancient city</h2>

<p>Nine hundred years ago, Cahokia occupied the same floodplain as Centreville does today. At its population peak around 1100 CE, over 100 burial, residential and ceremonial earthen mounds stretched from one end of the valley to the other, with its core centered on Monks Mound. </p>

<p><a href="https://cahokiamounds.org/mound/mound-38-monks-mound/">Monks Mound</a> is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. It is 950 feet (290 meters) long and 775 feet (236 meters) wide, and its platform rises 100 feet (30 meters) above the floodplain. Decades of archaeological excavation show that surrounding Monks Mound are plazas that held great feasts and possibly sporting events – including <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SpccDCKeQts">chunkey, something like bocce ball with spears</a> – <a href="https://www.history.com/articles/woodhenge-cahokia">timber monuments</a> likely for ritually observing astronomical events, and other mounds containing <a href="https://cahokiamounds.org/mound/mound-72/">elaborate burials</a>.</p>

<p><iframe id="3qQkc" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3qQkc/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map showing the relative locations of Centreville, Cahokia and St. Louis."></iframe></p>

<p>Possibly up to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia at the start of the 12th century, but by the end of the century, the city had entered a population decline that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2018.03.009">continued for 200 years</a>. Archaeologists have long debated the cause of Cahokia’s depopulation before European explorers and colonists arrived, putting forward a <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/publication/285045502_Contemplating_Cahokia's_Collapse">range of societal and environmental theories</a>.</p>

<h2>Climate change at Cahokia</h2>

<p>In other research, several colleagues and I previously found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1809400116">Cahokia experienced several natural disasters</a> during a warming period known as the <a href="https://theconversation.com/climate-explained-what-was-the-medieval-warm-period-155294">Medieval Climatic Anomaly</a>. In the second half of the 12th century, Cahokia experienced a large Mississippi River flood and drought conditions that stretched for several decades. Our study argued that the site’s depopulation was related to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1809400116">those climatic changes</a>.</p>

<p>Climate change at Cahokia didn’t look like <a href="https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/publications/before-and-after-the-day-after-tomorrow/">catastrophic scenes in movies like “The Day After Tomorrow</a>.” There’s no evidence to suggest widespread destruction or death. Departures began at a time that coincided with climatic changes of the 12th century, but people continued to gradually leave the site through the 13th and 14th centuries.</p>

<p>As people left, life in Cahokia changed. After 1200 CE, <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2694566">archaeological evidence</a> suggests Cahokians ceased or reduced communal feasting and mound building. They also contributed less to public granaries, moving agricultural surplus to private spaces. But it only became harder to live there for some people: <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2694421">Larger houses and status symbols</a> became more prevalent, perhaps indicating a larger gap between the rich and poor. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The past and future of climate change</h2>

<p>To understand the relationship between social and environmental changes at Cahokia, I look at what is happening at Centreville in the 21st century.  </p>

<p>People are not leaving all at once; instead, the accumulation of years of flooding-related failing infrastructure, repair costs and health problems have pushed some away from the community. Others have stayed, like resident William McNeal, who told a local news outlet, “<a href="https://www.stltoday.com/news/local/illinois/a-plea-for-help-centreville-s-sewage-and-drainage-problems-pose-health-safety-risks/article_3d6d22c7-8c57-5d1a-8af3-a6e6ee6ea2ee.html">I’m not going to abandon my house</a>. It’s all I got.” </p>

<p>Additionally, what’s happening in Centreville reveals that climate change is experienced unequally – some people are more affected than others. All of the St. Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure.</p>

<p>At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways. Those with farms in the lower floodplain were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaa.2026.101797">most exposed to crop loss from flooding</a>, but plots in the uplands were safer. During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils.</p>

<p>People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to <a href="https://doi.org/10.5876/9781607323808.c009">communal feasts</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2694421">shared food storage</a>. I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave. Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society. </p>

<p>If that’s what happened, climate change did not cause a sudden and dramatic exodus from Cahokia. Instead, its uneven effects altered the social status quo; <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/2694421">some benefited, some lost</a>, and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2018.03.009">some left</a>.</p>

<p>Today, some consequences of climate change can be major and immediate, such as <a href="https://theconversation.com/nepals-flash-floods-show-the-devastating-power-of-cascading-hazards-290611">sudden massive floods</a>. But in communities like Centreville, the effects of repeated flooding accumulate over years, producing gradual societal changes that are harder to recognize than the aftermath of a sudden catastrophe.</p>

<p>Climate models are useful for estimating future conditions, but they reveal nothing about how people might experience or respond to those conditions. Events and people’s reactions may unfold quickly, even suddenly, or they may play out quietly over long periods of time.</p>

<p>Regardless, the result may be the stillness of an archaeological site.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294435/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Sewing an infinity of phalluses – how Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama confronted the male-dominated art world by mocking it</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773992/original/file-20261124-62-dsp100.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C47%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Yayoi Kusama recreated and subverted the ubiquity of male symbolism in art. Shown here is her work &#39;Violet Obsession.&#39;</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/violet-obsession-part-of-yayoi-kusama-infinite-mirrors-news-photo/647003398">Bill O&#39;Leary/The Washington Post via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Japanese artist <a href="https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artists/yayoi-kusama-8094/introduction-yayoi-kusama">Yayoi Kusama’s</a> installations are big, bold and controversial. From the time she burst upon the <a href="https://www.tate.org.uk/art/art-terms/p/pop-art">pop art</a> scene in the 1960s until her death on Aug. 14, 2026, at the age of 97, she challenged the Western, male-dominated art world. She also upended assumptions about mental disorders, which many people have uncritically seen as the <a href="https://theconversation.com/before-the-infinity-nets-there-was-the-pacific-ocean-what-origin-stories-focusing-on-yayoi-kusamas-mental-illness-miss-about-her-art-290760">source of her creativity</a>. Her phallic sculptures and confounding mirror rooms are still popular, and they defy artistic classifications. </p>

<p>Kusama’s resistance to categorization raises an intriguing question: What is her lasting effect on the art world? </p>

<p>Kusama took a major step into the global art scene after sending two canvases for display at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum on Feb. 5, 1962. After that, she shifted her direction to avant-garde sculpture. She created <a href="https://www.moma.org/audio/playlist/297/4027">Accumulation No. 1</a>, her first work in a series that employed sewn phallic protrusions. The series thrust her into New York City’s pop art scene and would lead to her fantastical <a href="https://hirshhorn.si.edu/kusama/infinity-rooms/">Infinity Mirror Rooms</a> installation.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773978/original/file-20261124-76-rsfd2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Exhibit of Yayoi Kusama's work, featuring a chair, sofa, shelf, high-heeled shoes, suitcase and jacket covered in phallic protrusions" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773978/original/file-20261124-76-rsfd2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773978/original/file-20261124-76-rsfd2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=419&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773978/original/file-20261124-76-rsfd2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=419&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773978/original/file-20261124-76-rsfd2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=419&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773978/original/file-20261124-76-rsfd2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=526&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773978/original/file-20261124-76-rsfd2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=526&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773978/original/file-20261124-76-rsfd2.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=526&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Accumulation No. 1 is shown on the far left, among other similarly themed works.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/works-by-yayoi-kusama-on-display-at-the-yayoi-kusama-news-photo/148196135">J. Countess/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>A major retrospective of her work is <a href="https://www.stedelijk.nl/nl/tentoonstellingen/yayoi-kusama">on view at the Stedelijk Museum</a> through Jan. 17, 2027.</p>

<p>The specter of her mental health issues, however, still undermines her art’s significance. Critics often link the repetition in her work to obsessive-compulsive disorder. But as an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=zFzYmJwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">art historian</a> who has studied Kusama extensively, I argue that she intentionally used compulsivity to examine gender issues in the art world. A close look at Accumulation No. 1 reveals how she pulled this off.</p>

<h2>Phallic focus</h2>

<p>Kusama’s emphasis on gender came into focus when she arrived in the <a href="https://www.moma.org/calendar/exhibitions/3663">male-dominated New York art world</a>. During the 1940s and 50s, while abstract expressionism reigned in New York, women in the scene were treated as wives and assistants. </p>

<p>Painter <a href="https://www.moma.org/collection/works/78375">Grace Hartigan</a> had to adopt the pseudonym “George” to gain recognition. By the 1960s, that was starting to change. Venezuelan sculptor <a href="https://buffaloakg.org/person/marisol">Marisol Escobar’s May 1962 exhibition</a> at the Stable Gallery bucked the trend of gender conformity by integrating self-portraits into her sculpture series.</p>

<p>Kusama’s Accumulation No. 1 emerged as New York artists were seeking to move beyond <a href="https://www.britannica.com/art/Abstract-Expressionism">abstract expressionism</a>. The gestural paintings of this art movement were what some critics saw as an existential struggle toward originality <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/778410">coded as masculine</a>. Pop artists <a href="https://www.guggenheim-bilbao.eus/en/exhibition/gallery-303-echoes-of-pop-art">refused this model</a>: They turned instead to ready-made objects and impersonal repetition, evoking factory production. </p>

<p>Kusama procured furniture and egg cartons for her Accumulation sculptures, as well as a wooden rowboat for another sculpture that became <a href="https://www.moma.org/interactives/exhibitions/1998/kusama/manual/kusama_10.html">Aggregation One Thousand Boats Show</a>. She decided to focus on sewing — an art <a href="https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1390572174767769472">rooted in her female Japanese education</a> — and she ordered a sewing machine.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="White boat covered in white protrusions, set in a room patterned with the same image" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773975/original/file-20261124-62-1ixr2v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/this-photograph-shows-the-artwork-aggregation-one-thousand-news-photo/2293764340">Lina Selg / AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
