title: Trump just can’t quit tariffs
excerpt: President Donald Trump at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony at the White House on November 24, 2026. | Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images This stor
body: President Donald Trump at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony at the White House on November 24, 2026. | Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is trying to keep its trade war alive with new tariff announcements.  Who’s getting tariffed? Potentially dozens of countries, including China, the EU’s 27 member states, South Korea, and others
If they take effect, the China tariffs would start at 20 percent and could escalate to as high as 40 percent, while EU tariffs would start at 15 percent and could go up from there

How? The administration is justifying these tariffs on the basis of an investigation into what it alleges are unfair trade practices by the targeted countries — a step it’s taking only after its previous tariffs regime, which attempted to use emergency powers to impose tariffs, was struck down by the Supreme Court.  Despite Wednesday’s announcement, it’s still not entirely clear when the new tariffs will take effect; according to the US trade adviser , Jamieson Greer, it’s unlikely to be sooner than “a couple months from now.”  What’s the context? Courts have struck down two different attempts by the Trump administration to impose a global tariff regime, including the emergency authority the Supreme Court ruled on in February 2026.  Wednesday’s move is part of its attempt to reconstitute that regime using other authorities, joining a sweeping set of tariffs imposed in July over alleged forced-labor concerns
The US is also engaged in a specific trade fight with Canada: In August, President Donald Trump imposed  50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods after trade talks fell through

Why does this matter? Tariffs, as my colleague Eric Levitz has reported , don’t work the way the president seems to think; his project is based on a fundamentally incorrect understanding of economics that’s making things more expensive for American consumers.  Despite that fact, Wednesday’s announcement suggests he’s doubling down, despite persistently high inflation , and undeterred by his crushing midterms defeat earlier this month, when voters motivated by affordability turned out to deliver a historic rebuke

And with that, it’s time to log off… Hi readers, happy early Thanksgiving! This will be our last newsletter for the week — the Vox team is taking some time off to be with our families today and tomorrow, and we’ll see you back here on Monday.  Before we go, I have one more story to share from my colleague Jonquilyn Hill, who wrote about the best way to strategically approach your Thanksgiving dinner for maximum enjoyment (subjective, yes, but she asked a gastroenterologist for some tips)
Plus: Why it’s not really the turkey that’s making you so sleepy

title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s deportation saga ends on his terms
excerpt: Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrives at the US District Court for the District of Maryland with his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, and his attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshen
body: Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrives at the US District Court for the District of Maryland with his wife, Jennifer Vasquez Sura, and his attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, on December 22, 2025, in Greenbelt, Maryland. | Alex Wong/Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland man who was wrongly deported and then indicted by the Trump administration, has left the US on his own terms, after more than a year of legal struggles that became emblematic of the administration’s often cruel and haphazard immigration policy

Abrego Garcia arrived in Madrid, Spain, on Wednesday, after choosing to “self-deport” to a country of his choice, rather than one of the African nations to which the Trump administration was trying to send him

It’s the conclusion — for now — of a saga that began in March 2025, when Abrego Garcia was arrested by ICE and sent to an infamous megaprison in El Salvador. (Abrego Garcia is Salvadoran and does not have US citizenship, though he’s married to a US citizen.) At the time of his deportation, ICE was legally barred from returning him to El Salvador because of threats to his life there

Nevertheless, the Trump administration resisted returning him to the US for multiple months — and upon his return, indicted him on human smuggling charges that a judge later described as “an abuse of prosecuting power” in an opinion dismissing the charges in May 2026
After those charges were dismissed, the administration attempted to deport Abrego García to a third country — but refused to allow him to leave for Costa Rica, which had said it would accept him
Instead, administration officials sought to send him to four different African countries to which he has no connection: Eswatini, Ghana, Liberia, and Uganda

After failing to do so, however, it acceded last weekto Abrego Garcia’s departure to Spain, which he entered Wednesday on a temporary tourist visa. “I am leaving with my freedom, and I am not leaving the way they removed me before, in a practically inhumane manner,” Abrego Garcia said on Wednesday after he arrived, according to CNN . “My family and I will choose the next steps.” Trump’s ongoing deportations campaign Abrego Garcia’s story attracted attention for being unusually tortuous, specific, and personal — but his departure doesn’t settle anything about the bigger issue, or the thousands of less well-known people in his situation
The Trump administration hasn’t abandoned its policy of punitive deportations, often to countries with serious human rights concerns

In fact,  as Wired explained on Wednesday , it’s “expanded into a signature White House policy of mass removal,” including deals with 35 countries to accept US deportees and tens of thousands of deportations

In some cases, the US is paying those countries to accept migrants — and some of those countries are so inhospitable they appear on the State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list.  Eswatini (formerly Swaziland), where the administration attempted to send Abrego Garcia, is one of those countries
Other migrants have been sent there, according to Wired , including Pheap Rom, a Cambodian refugee who was imprisoned in Eswatini until earlier this year, when he was returned to Cambodia

It’s a policy the Trump administration intends to continue: It’s  currently asking the Supreme Court to allow it to continue removals to third countries despite the Convention Against Torture , which prevents deportations “in which there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture.” The Court will hear the case early next month, on December 9
One link for later ➨ Get your gratitude on
Giving thanks is the literal name of the game this week, but it has benefits year-round
Research shows that a habit as simple as jotting down a couple things you’re grateful for each week can make you a happier and — intriguingly — more altruistic person
Before you go… Did you know… that Thanksgiving was first declared a national holiday in the US during the Civil War? It was seen as a way to both advance family values and bring Americans together

That would be a supermoon, and if you were looking up last night, you might have glimpsed the beaver supermoon (a beaver moon is just November’s full moon).

title: Why the Army detonated toxic explosives in Iowa
excerpt: A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on November 19, 2026. | Scott Olson/Getty Im
body: A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on November 19, 2026. | Scott Olson/Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

On Wednesday, the Pentagon blew up about five tons of lead azide, an unstable explosive stored at an ammunition plant in Iowa, in order to dispose of it, sending a toxic plume of lead dust into the sky the day before Thanksgiving
The detonation was briefly halted by a lower court before a federal circuit court cleared the way on Monday, and went forward despite serious public health concerns

There was a real need for haste, according to the Army : The lead azide was sufficiently unstable that it was at risk of detonating on its own in an uncontrolled explosion, and falling temperatures in Iowa reportedly made such an explosion more likely
An uncontrolled explosion would have be more dangerous and unpredictable, and could have caused worse lead pollution

At the same time, though, Iowa residents are angry and alarmed by a lack of clear information, poor communication by the Army, and the potential health hazards.  The potential for things to go sideways had President Donald Trump nervous enough that he tried to pass the decision to Rob Sand — not the current Iowa governor, but the incoming Democratic governor-elect — and let any consequences fall on his head

The lead plume produced by the blast — which will take place inside reinforced concrete bunkers, along with other steps to mitigate the risk — could still spread as far as 100 miles from the site, according to the Washington Post .  The American Lung Association has urged anyone near the blast to remain inside for one to two days afterward, among other guidance, and on Tuesday, the Health and Human Services Department recommended that children and pregnant women evacuate from the path of the plume, which could stretch into neighboring Missouri

The lead risk all around us Emergency munitions detonations in the US are pretty rare — there are, thankfully, better ways to dispose of toxic materials these days (and questions about why the Army didn’t pursue them in this case).  But despite a great deal of progress in the US — including banning things like new lead paint and pipes and leaded gasoline in the 20th century — lead remains a serious public health threat.  Part of that is because of how dangerous it really is: Lead is not just a neurotoxin, but one with no safe levels of human exposure; even a little bit can be harmful, especially to children.  But as my colleague Dylan Scott  reported in 2024, it also keeps popping up nearly everywhere we look, including in our food supply.  According to Dylan’s reporting , there are three big reasons for lead’s seeming inescapability: Active disregard, negligence, and the fact that it’s just really hard to get rid of

Lead was widely used in the US decades ago, before those bans on lead paint and leaded gasoline, and some of that lead is still around, in the soil, in old houses, and in other materials dating back to that time

It’s also not a problem that the US can easily address alone, since lots of lead exposure is the result of goods being imported into the US.  “If we really want to solve this,” Drew McCartor, the director of a global public health nonprofit, told Dylan at the time, “it requires a whole-­of-­government commitment to work outside of our borders.” One link for later ➨ Follow “Maslow’s hierarchy of hosting.” Thanksgiving is almost upon us, and if you’re feeling a little angsty about your holiday obligations, consider this guidance from the event planner Megan Fitzgerald: Your hosting needs, at a minimum, start with a clean space, a bathroom stocked with adequate toilet paper, and enough cups and water to go around. (Plus, of course, the food.) Basically, everything else is extra

Before you go… Did you know… that, with very few exceptions, US grocery stores sell only one breed of turkey ? It’s called the Broad Breasted White turkey, and it’s been bred to grow twice as fast (and become nearly twice as big) as its forebears did in the 1960s

Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday, we asked you which 19th-century author and activist is known as “the mother of Black feminism.” That would be Anna Julia Cooper, who was one of the first African American women to receive a PhD
She lived to 105, well into the 20th century

title: How to approach gifting so you don’t go broke, hurt anyone’s feelings, or end up drowning in crap
excerpt: You don’t need me to tell you it’s expensive out there — groceries and gas cost a fortune, inflation is still hot hot hot , and getting a raise? Maybe nex
body: You don’t need me to tell you it’s expensive out there — groceries and gas cost a fortune, inflation is still hot hot hot , and getting a raise? Maybe next year, babe.  If this is relatable for you, you might be dreading the holidays
Maybe not the celebrations, exactly, but the gift giving of it all — all the spending, all the stuff
Between the cost to your bank account and the cost to the planet, I wouldn’t blame you if the thought of holiday gifting was causing some angst right now.  “The holidays are already stressful
Even if we think they’re fun, there’s a lot of stress associated with it,” financial therapist Lindsay Bryan-Podvin tells Vox
With higher prices on gas, groceries, travel, and eating out, “it’s compounding.” It doesn’t have to be torturous, though
With the right approach, you can get your loved ones on board with a lower-cost, lower-waste holiday season
It just takes creativity and a little finesse
Set your budget for gifts So, you know you want to do things differently this season but you’re still planning to do some gifting
The first step? Make a budget, Bryan-Podvin says
A pro tip for next year Once you get through the chaos of this season, think about setting up a budget for gifting in January or February
Bryan-Podvin has a sinking fund called “Gifts” that she adds to every month
When a gifting occasion hits, she looks to that account to see how much she can afford to spend. “Whatever’s in there helps direct how much I will or won’t spend,” she says
To set this up, see if your savings account offers a “bucketing” feature — a way to subdivide your savings account by goal — or an option to open multiple savings accounts without fees or minimums
Then, allocate one bucket or savings account to gift giving, and set up a regular auto-deposit amount
You can always open a savings account with another bank, like Ally or Capital One, if your current bank doesn’t offer one of these options
Here’s what she suggests: Decide what feels like a comfortable amount to spend — where you won’t feel anxious or resentful — and use that as your holiday budget
Don’t add up the cost of all the gifts you want to buy and then try to make that work with credit cards and buy-now-pay-later apps
You are the one making your budget — your budget is not being decided for you

Set that dollar amount, and then shop, craft, bake, scavenge, and forage within it.  If your gifting anxiety is more about consumerism, climate change, and the desire to give less stuff, now is also the time to think about an approach you would be comfortable with
Maybe you only want to give gifts to the kids in your life, or propose that your large extended family pull names from a hat instead of getting each person their own present
Perhaps your family would be excited to try an experience together, like going to a holiday light show and getting hot chocolate afterward, instead of exchanging presents
Whatever strategy you land on, keeping a guiding principle in mind for your holiday spending will help you stay grounded when the Black Friday sales hit

It’s your budget and your holiday season — you get to decide what it looks like.   Set expectations with your friends and family Culturally, many people feel that expectations around holiday gifting — not to mention traveling, hosting, and decorating — are rising, Bryan-Podvin says. “Gift giving has really expanded beyond giving within a family,” she says. “It seems like every group is doing a gift exchange, whether it’s your tennis club, your PTA group. … It might be well intentioned, but it’s also adding a lot of pressure.” The data backs that up: A new Gallup poll found that around a third of Americans still expect to spend more than $1,000 on holiday gifts in 2026, the highest figure recorded in the past 20 years.  But according to etiquette expert Lizzie Post , co-president at the Emily Post Institute, stepping back from the gift exchange — whether it’s within a social group or your family — is a perfectly acceptable thing to do

Don’t have the money this year? Don’t have the energy to plan, shop, and wrap? Anxious about adding to the landfill with unloved gifts? All it takes is a phone call to the person in charge to let them know.  “Try not to predict their reaction in [your] initial outreach,” she tells Vox. “Just say, ‘Hey, I’ve been so grateful that you’ve put this together each and every year, and John and I just aren’t going to be able to participate this year.’” That’s it — just be clear, candid, and grateful for the effort they’ve put in to organize the gift exchange
You can’t control someone else’s reaction, Post says.  Same goes for your family members, whether it’s a group thing or a one-on-one exchange

Just give each of them a call and be honest: “I won’t be able to do our gift exchange this year, but I can’t wait to jump back in down the road.” Post says she thinks hurt feelings are unlikely; most people understand times are tight right now
If you’re choosing to give differently this year — only edible gifts, things you’ve crafted yourself, or secondhand items, for example — that’s also something you can share if it feels necessary
Just follow the same advice: Be clear, be confident, and don’t feel the need to apologize

And if you’re worried about the etiquette of declining to participate or participating in a different way, don’t: Post says it’s fine for traditions to change, evolve, or even pause over time. “Not every year is going to be a year you can partake in something like that,” she says. “You don’t punish people for these moments, you work with them.” How to feel really good about the gifts you’re giving One important thing to keep in mind when you’re gathering presents this year: Gifting should feel good
Thinking about your loved ones, considering what they’ll actually like and use…that’s what it’s all about
Don’t let the targeted ads get in your head — there are many ways to give gifts that don’t involve spending a fortune on random novelty gifts or tchotchkes

Megan Gray, senior shopping writer at Apartment Therapy , tells Vox she always makes a gift-giving list and checks it off, focusing on scoring deals and buying on sale rather than randomly buying things for people. “Try to give a few minutes’ thought to each person,” she says, then write down what you’d like to get for them. “That always helps more than just going to the internet and searching. … That’s where you’re going to forget and put it off and then you’re going to have to do it last-minute, and that’s where you spend the money and get the gifts that aren’t going to resonate.” To build your list, use one of these practical strategies to spend less money, generate less waste, and ultimately give more meaningful items
Give subscriptions, memberships, or experiences Subscriptions can be a meaningful way to give someone a year-long experience you know they’ll enjoy
For example, if you have a friend who loves to cook, give them a subscription to a recipe site like New York Times Cooking or America’s Test Kitchen
Have a sibling with kids? Give their family a membership to the local children’s museum, zoo, or science center
A radio-nerd bestie? Turn them into a This American Life partner for ad-free listening and bonus content
A cinema-loving partner? Gift them a year-long subscription to the Criterion Channel

Going this route also allows you to get more bang for your buck; a great board game or a family membership to a museum is likely going to be more meaningful and less expensive than buying each of your nieces and nephews a toy

Like subscriptions and memberships, experiential gifts are a nice option for gift giving that doesn’t involve actual stuff (though they can be pricey, so you may want to avoid this if your budget is really tight)

Event tickets and gift cards are a stellar idea here: sports, theater, concerts, live dance shows, Disney on Ice, cooking classes, luxury movie tickets with seat-side service, a wine tasting at the bar down the street, a stand-up comedy show — all are great ways to show you’ve thought about your loved one and their interests

title: Stop eating turkey and start enjoying Thanksgiving
excerpt: A turkey rescued from becoming meat is celebrated on Thanksgiving at the Gentle Barn animal sanctuary in California in 2025. | Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Time
body: A turkey rescued from becoming meat is celebrated on Thanksgiving at the Gentle Barn animal sanctuary in California in 2025. | Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images I haven’t eaten turkey in many years, and a large share of Americans who have it on Thanksgiving would rather eat something else , too
That turkey is the most overrated part of this glorious long weekend between the end of summer and the winter holidays has become a cultural bit as familiar as the dead bird itself

As the journalist Brian McManus wrote for Vice : “It is, almost without fail, a dried-out, depressing hunk of sun-baked papier-mâché — a jaw-tiringly chewy, unsatisfying, and depressingly bland workout.” “Throw it in the garbage,” The Guardian commanded about the Thanksgiving turkey a decade ago
That’s indeed what happens to many of them — perhaps their culinary mediocrity is part of why the equivalent of well over 8 million turkeys are thrown away as food waste on Thanksgiving
This is all very strange, and sad, too, because life is too short to eat bad food on holidays — and the Thanksgiving turkey isn’t a mere harmless tradition

I know it’s untoward and uncool to talk about where our meat comes from at the holiday table, but putting millions of birds through hell for a dish many people can’t stop complaining about seems like a particularly concerning situation
Turkeys are factory-farmed in the second-largest numbers of any animal in the US, after chickens

Most spend their short lives packed by the thousands into crowded sheds , where the stress can drive them to attack one another; to prevent this, producers cut off parts of their beaks and toes without pain relief
The animals have been bred to grow so large, so fast — their weight has doubled since 1960 — that many struggle to even walk
Like other farmed animals, they don’t even reproduce naturally (more details of how that works on turkey farms, if you can stomach it, can be found here )

I could go on, but surely that’s reason enough to try some different holiday traditions? I have lots of experience cooking and eating on Thanksgiving sans turkey in mixed company (that is, with both committed vegans and lifelong carnivores)

Here are some of my favorite, satisfying, crowd-pleasing centerpieces to make instead:  Mushroom Wellington Everyone was blown away by this plant-based version of a beef Wellington , which my made at last year’s Thanksgiving
It’s a variation on the New York Times’s vegetarian mushroom Wellington

The buttery (yes, even in the vegan version) puff pastry combined with the deep umami and sweet notes of several types of mushrooms and caramelized onions make it a gloriously rich main course that stands on its own and doesn’t feel like a plant-based imitation of something else
The filling can take quite a bit of time to prepare, but certainly less than the ordeal required to make a turkey taste good
I love the port reduction that accompanies the New York Times version, but it can also be served with a mushroom gravy , a red wine and shallot gravy , or any other sauce you like

Also, if you’re concerned that this is not a very high-protein dish (mushrooms are extremely high in water and aren’t a high-protein food), I promise you’ll get enough protein from the other dishes on the table, and eating one meal without maximizing protein intake won’t do you any harm
But if you do want a protein-packed entrée, there are many options to consider! For this one, I may try adding beans or lentils to the filling in the future
Creamy lentil bake I’ve had wonderful experiences making this recipe on holidays

The cashew cream on top, combined with tahini and balsamic flavor in the lentils, make it impossible to stop eating. (Cashew cream, if you’ve never had it, is one of the greatest magic tricks of plant-based cooking.) This lentil shepherd’s pie is a similar concept that’s also excellent and great for those with nut allergies (it does contain sesame, though)
Stuffed squash I couldn’t make this list without mentioning the option of stuffed squash or pumpkin, a beautiful classic of plant-based holiday fare
I haven’t made one of these in years, but there are endless recipe options online with hundreds of glowing reviews
Chickpea cutlets My family has been making these wonderfully firm, dense, chewy patties for many years
Developed by Isa Chandra Moskowitz, the undisputed queen of vegan cooking , the secret to their texture is wheat gluten , which has been used in Asian cuisines for centuries as a meat substitute
Gluten is one of the highest-protein things you can eat — I’m honestly not sure what distinguishes it from protein powder

Barbecue ribs For a slightly non-traditional but still distinctly American detour from the usual Thanksgiving flavors, try these plant-based ribs , also made with gluten, by Miyoko Schinner (this same recipe is also found in Schinner’s cookbook, The Homemade Vegan Pantry )
They were so good on the Fourth of July the past few years that we decided to turn them into a Thanksgiving main this year
Super easy mode: Store-bought plant-based roasts I know these can be polarizing, but they’ve gotten a lot better since the rubbery meat substitutes of yore
My favorite is Field Roast’s hazelnut and cranberry roast , which is wrapped in flaky puff pastry — kinda like a Wellington — followed by Gardein’s turk’y roast , which has a crispy breaded crust
There are plenty that I haven’t tried too: Juicy Marbles’s whole-cut loin is exceptionally well regarded, though pricey
My own turkey alternative list is long: I haven’t even gotten to this tried-and-true lentil meatloaf or the creamy baked wild rice with carrots from Nisha Vora’s doorstopper Big Vegan Flavor
For most of us, there’s an extraordinary abundance of food to be grateful for on Thanksgiving — the least we could do is extend a little of that good fortune to turkeys.

title: The paradox of Latino ICE agents
excerpt: Under the second Trump administration, immigration enforcement agencies have undergone a significant expansion
body: Under the second Trump administration, immigration enforcement agencies have undergone a significant expansion
President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill raised ICE’s budget from $10 billion to $85 billion, making it the most funded law enforcement agency in the United States
With that funding, they began offering economic incentives like signing bonuses and student loan forgiveness programs

The number of ICE agents and officers doubled in just one year , with another recruiting push underway through the end of 2026.  Today, perhaps more than ever, the front lines of those federal immigration law enforcement agencies reflect the demographics of the populations they were created to police
Latinos are overrepresented in the Department of Homeland Security , which houses ICE and Border Patrol
Self-identified Latinos account for nearly half of Border Patrol agents and about 30 percent of ICE agents

So why do so many Latinos join the immigration enforcement agencies that have targeted their own communities? The answers reveal complexities about American Latino identity and the splintered points of view on immigration policy at the border.  Hosted by Kahlil Greene , this video is part of our new series, Kahlil Explains, that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society

This episode traces the evolution of immigration enforcement agencies and their appeal to Latino recruits, to explain why so many ICE and Border Patrol agents are Latino.  Read and watch more about the Latino community and immigration enforcement: Geraldo Cadava’s writing for The Atlantic David Cortez’s research article Latinxs in La Migra: Why They Join and Why It Matters Irene Vega’s book, Bordering on Indifference: How Immigration Agents Negotiate Race and Morality   Vox’s video explaining immigration before ICE in America AtlasIntel’s 2026 USA Midterms Latino Poll Director Maisie Crow’s documentary At The Ready (Gravitas Ventures)

title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
excerpt: Need for speed: Data center developers are bypassing years-long grid connection waits by building their own private natural gas power plants
body: Need for speed: Data center developers are bypassing years-long grid connection waits by building their own private natural gas power plants
Over 100 such facilities have been announced in the US since early 2025, with combined capacity exceeding 115 gigawatts
A dirtier shortcut: If all planned US projects proceed, they could emit 152 million metric tons more CO₂ annually than if those data centers were grid connected, according to BloombergNEF tracking

Fossil fuel lock-in is a real risk: Though developers pitch private gas plants as temporary bridges until grid connections come through, experts warn that once built, operators are unlikely to simply switch them off—potentially cementing decades of fossil fuel dependency
Everyone else pays the price: Going off-grid doesn't insulate communities from the fallout

Greater natural gas demand could drive up fuel prices, squeezing the roughly 60% of American households that rely on it for heating and cooking. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149622" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade

Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.   xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024
At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators
It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles
But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company
The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California
The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025
It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today
But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy
When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator

That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability
Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them
Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants

These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation
Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however

Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.  Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.  The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions
Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation

That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)  Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand

Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.  Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines
These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build
Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says

That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.  BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US

If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report

That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.  And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation
More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking
That effect may also trickle into electricity prices
There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone
Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data
Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says

Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.  While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds

In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels. “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
excerpt: A legendary philosopher calls out Anthropic: Thomas Nagel, whose 1974 bat essay helped define consciousness studies, criticized openness to AI sentience as "com
body: A legendary philosopher calls out Anthropic: Thomas Nagel, whose 1974 bat essay helped define consciousness studies, criticized openness to AI sentience as "completely idiotic." But the belief isn't totally fringe: In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious

Form versus function: The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI
There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences

Anthropic's business model could be its own trap: If the company ever concluded its AI models were truly sentient, running them around the clock in data centers—and shutting them down—would become a moral catastrophe, one the company itself flagged as an investor risk. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149569" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here
Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing

Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.  Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.  This thinking isn’t all that fringe
According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have

In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).  But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place
Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat
Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat
But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know
Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer
You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness

In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.  The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI
There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week

Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet
Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course
This is still a philosophical question for now
But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York
He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?” It has to do with language

An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience

Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.  Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin
Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines
If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place
Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers

This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement
But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right
AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield
The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers
Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether

If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process
Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size
But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.
